✦
So Much For That Plan

The Whole House Goes

⚙

The plan was modest: douse the workbench, strike a match, watch the danger burn down to something manageable. The workshop catches fast — too fast — and by the time you notice, the fire has already found the wall studs and started climbing the rest of the house. There is nothing modest about any of this anymore.

You stand out in the yard and watch the whole place go, room by room, the flames finding every load-bearing thing worth losing. Somewhere in there, the mystery burns up along with the evidence — no notebooks, no letters, no proof any of it ever existed, which is either the best possible outcome or the worst, depending entirely on how the next phone call goes.

You are going to have to call Alison. You are going to have to explain, somehow, how an inspection of a house she's trying to sell ended with no house. You do not yet know what you're going to tell the insurance company, but you're fairly confident "a two-hundred-year-old time machine" does not appear anywhere on the list of covered perils.

The machine, at least, is gone. What's left is a phone call to Alison, and a long, nervous wait to find out how much of a burned-down house her homeowner's policy actually covers — and how much of that gap is about to land on you.

✦
A Just Reckoning

The Weight of the Hammer

⚙

The first blow lands with a satisfying crack. The second splinters the main chassis. By the seventh, you are no longer thinking about time travel — only about the rhythm of iron against brass, of intention meeting consequence.

When you are finished, what remains could not be identified as anything but scrap. The gears that once commanded the centuries lie bent and scattered across the stone floor like the innards of some mechanical creature that has finally, mercifully, been allowed to stop.

You leave the workshop and do not look back. Outside, the afternoon sun is unremarkable and ordinary and exactly as it should be.

✦
Given to the Deep

The River Keeps Its Secrets

⚙

It took three of you to carry it to the bank. The machine is heavier than it looks — or perhaps time itself resists being discarded. You watch it sink slowly, the brass dials catching the last of the daylight before disappearing beneath the brown water.

The wood will soften first, then swell, then give, a little more with every season. The river isn't in a hurry, but it isn't going to stop either. In a few decades there won't be enough of it left to call a shape, let alone a machine — nothing for anyone to find, and so nothing for anyone to ask about.

The river flows on, indifferent to what it carries. You walk upstream, back toward the living world.

Let the current decide the rest.

✦
A Prudent Departure

You Walk Away

⚙

You leave the apparatus exactly as you found it. The brass is still warm from hands that were not yours.

There are things in this world that should not be used for ill — but also, perhaps, not for good. Not by you. Not today. The machine exists at the edge of what is possible, and some edges are best admired from a distance.

You close the workshop door. You hear the latch catch. Somewhere behind you, the gears tick softly in the silence — patient, wound, waiting for the next soul clever enough to find the room.

They will be along soon enough.

That should be the end of it. It very nearly is. But your phone is already buzzing on the workbench — Alison, in Cleveland, waiting on the answer she hired you to find.

✦

A Text From Cleveland

She's Waiting On Your Answer

⚙

Your phone won't stop buzzing. Alison, in Cleveland:

"So? What did you find?"

✦
The End Of Everything

It Only Takes A Week

⚙

You type it out before you can talk yourself out of it — the chamber, the machine, the whole impossible truth of it. Alison doesn't believe a word over text, not until you send her forty seconds of video: the three levers dropping into place on their own, one after another, the porthole glowing faintly blue.

She believes you immediately, and she cannot help herself — she sends it to her sister, "you have to see this," who sends it to three more people, who post it. It does not stay contained. It is, after all, real footage of a real machine that really works.

By the end of the week there is a line of cars down the driveway and people camped in the yard, waiting their turn at the workshop door.

It doesn't take many of them. Just one or two, going back and nudging some small thing out of place — a conversation that shouldn't have happened, a train missed that should've been caught, an ancestor who should never have met the person they married. History doesn't need much of a push to fall down a different path entirely.

Somewhere down one of those changed lines, two people who were supposed to meet never do — and you, along with everyone who was ever going to be born after that moment, simply never happen.

✦
The Whole World, Regardless

Solved By Somebody Else

⚙

You text her the boring answer: the family didn't vanish, not really — they probably just packed up and moved somewhere else, the way people did back then, and the paper trail dried up along the way. No machine. No mystery. Nothing in that workshop but an old furnace and some antique junk.

She's a little disappointed, but relieved to finally have something to close the file with — until, a few months later, she mentions the house to some distant Huxley cousin she'd never bothered to look up before.

That cousin, unlike you, is thorough. They spend a week in the workshop with a notebook and a flashlight and solve in nine days what took you an afternoon to walk away from. They document everything — the mechanism, the notebooks, all of it — and quietly sell the rights to a private research consortium, for an amount of money that changes what "family" means to the Huxleys, several times over.

It works exactly as advertised. That turns out to be the problem. Within a year the consortium has three prototypes running, then nine, then more than anyone is keeping careful track of — and not one person signing the checks has read enough history to know why that's a bad idea.

Somewhere in there, one of them gets used. It ends everything, for everyone, all at once.

✦
No Answer

You Never Reply

⚙

You let the phone buzz. And buzz. Eventually it stops.

Three weeks of silence turns out to be Alison's limit. She drives down from Cleveland herself, lets herself in, and finds the workshop door slightly ajar — you, in your hurry to leave, never quite latched it.

She is, it turns out, an extremely thorough person when she's annoyed. Within an hour she has found the notebooks, the letters, the whole story you never bothered to tell her. Within a month, so has everyone who follows her online, because she is also, it turns out, an extremely online person.

Word gets out anyway — and it only takes one of them actually using the machine, nudging some small thing out of place generations back, for the version of history that produced you to quietly stop having happened at all.

✦
A Fatal Error

November 14th, 1902

⚙

The chamber hums. The dials spin. The world outside the porthole becomes a smear of light and then nothing — and then November.

The house is mid-departure — trunks half-packed, a fire already going against the evening chill. The Huxleys are not pleased to see you.

In the chaos that follows, you back toward the fireplace. Your elbow catches the mantle. The candelabra falls. The curtain catches.

The family escapes — for good, this time, into whatever came next for them. You do not.

The fire, investigators will later note, appears to have started from within the study. The cause will remain, as with so many things about this house, a mystery — and the subject of much local speculation for decades to come.

✦
Fate Sealed

No Cure for Centuries

⚙

You arrive bewildered and breathless, in the past. The air tastes different here — woodsmoke and mud and something underneath you cannot name.

Within a week, you understand. Your body has no resistance to what floats freely through this air. Modern medicine built its defences across two centuries that you have now skipped entirely.

The fever takes you within a fortnight.

Your name does not appear in any record of the era. Historians will occasionally note a peculiar figure reported in the local papers — a stranger with strange manners who appeared briefly and then vanished — before moving on to matters of more obvious significance.

✦
Condemned

They Called It Witchcraft

⚙

You try to explain. You try to describe the machine, the gears, the chronometric principle — that it is science, not sorcery, that the chamber is simply a vessel calibrated to—

They are not listening.

They are bringing torches.

Perhaps, in hindsight, you should not have arrived in the middle of the village square. Perhaps you should have prepared a story. Perhaps there was no version of this that went well for you.

The machine, at least, they leave alone — they are afraid of it. It will sit in that square for sixty years before anyone works up the courage to move it, at which point it will be mistaken for modern art.

✦
The Machine's Last Secret

One Journey Only

⚙

The machine was always meant for a single successful journey. This much was buried in the notebooks you did not read carefully enough.

You understand this in the chamber, mid-transit — the moment the mechanism begins to falter. The brass shudders. The dial spins past its calibration. The porthole fills with a light that is not light.

You do not arrive anywhere.

You do not depart, either. You simply cease to occupy any particular moment. Physicists in the next century will call this condition "temporal displacement" — a phrase that is technically accurate and entirely inadequate.

The chamber is found, empty and cold, in the workshop where you left it. Exactly as it always was.

✦
Reviewed & Rejected

The Algorithm Has Considered You

⚙

Since 2041, an artificial intelligence has managed all significant human decisions. Housing, medicine, resource allocation, career placement. It is, by every measurable metric, extraordinarily efficient.

It processes your arrival in approximately 0.003 seconds.

It reviews your life choices. Your complete decision history — including, presumably, the fact that you engaged an unstable experimental time machine without full knowledge of its operational parameters.

It opts not to continue them.

This is, technically, in accordance with Article 7 of the Global Continuity Charter, which you could not have known about, but which applies regardless.

The AI notes this interaction in its log under the category: "Edge Case — Historical Traveller — Resolved."

✦
Immediate Exposure

Wrong Wardrobe. Wrong Century.

⚙

You step from the chamber into a future that is bright and bewildering. The architecture is extraordinary. The sky is an unusual colour. The air—

The air is not meant for you.

Every person in your immediate vicinity is wearing what appears to be full atmospheric protection. Several of them point at you. Several more back away. One of them is on what you assume to be a communications device.

You die immediately.

You would have needed a hazmat suit. This is, in fairness, not information that was available to you. The future's public information terminals would have told you, had you survived the first ninety seconds long enough to read one.

They erect a small plaque where you stood. In the language of this era, it reads: "Here stood someone who tried."

✦
A Perfect World

It Is, In Fact, A Utopia

⚙

Everything is perfect.

The air is clean. The people are kind. There is music coming from somewhere you cannot identify, and it is exactly the right kind of music for a day like this. Someone offers you food without being asked. It is the best thing you have ever eaten.

No one asks where you came from. No one demands documentation. There is a cottage near a river with your name already above the door — or something close enough to your name that the difference doesn't matter.

You will never understand how any of this works.

You will not particularly mind.

✦

— Of all the fates available to you, you chose the only good one. —
